Note: this was searched via WebSearch only (9 searches). Several results disagree with each other or carry mislabeled dates, so figures are provisional.

1. Why stocks are lower (11-24)
- Chip/AI weakness is the main reported driver (Yahoo Finance live blog, Invezz, Investing.com). Nasdaq opened ~1.6% lower, and intraday readings of -1.3% to -1.8% were reported. Headlines framed it as "Nvidia rally fades" and "investors test Nvidia-fueled rally."
- Rates: coverage cites renewed rate-hike expectations and this week's inflation reading as the last big data point before the December Fed meeting (BigGo, summary of search).
- Benzinga attributed futures weakness to Bessent unveiling fresh Iran sanctions and Hormuz warnings. A separate search could not confirm this.
- Context from sources: Friday 11-20 the S&P entered correction territory; Monday it closed 7,237.17 (+4.73%).
- Nvidia follow-ups: Reuters and Nvidia's 8-K (11-23) say the board voted unanimously after input from senior US government levels, and Trump publicly backed the move. Both parties criticized Trump's role (Schumer among them). An independent board committee's investigation continues.
- SEC: the WSJ reported a civil inquiry into Nvidia disclosures (Singapore sales). The SEC would not confirm. Date not found.

2. AI names this morning
- Nvidia about -5% after +31% Monday. Micron -8%, AMD -9%, Broadcom -4% (summary of Investing.com, Yahoo Finance). Reasons given: fading rally, rate fears. Intraday figures only.

3. Background
- 11-12: Nvidia announced Huang's resignation. Colette Kress became interim CEO and Harvey Jones became chair. The board cited personal conduct violating the code of conduct. Reuters described extramarital affairs.
- Earnings call (about 11-17, per sources): Jones said the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen." Huang said he would be "honoured" to return. Nvidia fell more than 10% after his exit.
- Weekend: Trump-brokered reversal reported. 8-K dated 11-23.

4. Scheduled events
- Not found for 2026. Only Thanksgiving timing is known. The Fed's calendar page showed a possible 11-25 statistical release, but the snippet was jumbled.
- By pattern from prior years, Wednesday would carry jobless claims, durable goods and GDP revision, and a 20-year auction may be early in the week. Treat these as unverified.

5. Strategists on "relief rally being sold"
- No named strategist quotes found for 11-23 or 11-24. Yahoo Finance says it is "testing" the rally. Fool.com and 24/7 Wall St ran pieces on the correction and the record point gain.

Most likely explanation for this morning's fall
- Partial profit-taking and fading of Monday's one-day Nvidia-driven relief rally, which closed below its open, amid chip weakness and rate and inflation worries, with possible geopolitical news (Iran and Hormuz) on top. Confidence: medium-low, because no source explicitly attributes it to profit-taking and the news-flow evidence is mixed.

Could not verify
- Named strategist commentary
- 2026 data, auction and Fed-speaker schedule
- Final or exact morning index levels
- SEC inquiry date or confirmation
- The Bessent and Iran item
- Any conditions attached to Huang's reinstatement or board changes
- Which news stories are stale: several results are 2024-25 and were discarded.
- Exact date of the board statement: sources say it came on the earnings call, while your brief says 11-17 (the AP item dated 11-17 mentions earnings, and the 11-12 resignation date is from Nvidia's release).

finding.preregistration: Written at the top of study.py before any outcome was computed. gap = Open_t/Close_{t-1}-1. z = gap divided by the stock's 20-day close-to-close standard deviation, using only days before t. oc = Close_t/Open_t-1. fwdK = Close_{t+K}/Close_t-1 for K = 1, 3, 5. zprior = the previous day's close-to-close return divided by the same sigma. Excess = the raw return minus the same symbol's unconditional mean for that horizon in the same sample, which strips out survivorship drift. Hit = % of raw returns above 0, always shown beside the unconditional hit rate. Universes are SPY, QQQ and STOCKS (125 equities). The six short-history names are kept, and the 18 listed series are excluded. t-statistics are clustered by date: stocks are averaged per event date, then t is taken over dates. Episodes are event dates at least 10 sessions apart. Splits: 15 days with a close-to-close move beyond +/-45% were dropped, together with any forward window spanning them. Grid: 12 gap buckets (z beyond +/-1, 2, 3; gap beyond +/-2%, 4%, 8%) x 3 universes for same-day oc = 36. The same buckets split by close above or below the open x fwd1/3/5 x 3 universes = 216. Snap-back cells (gap z>+1 after zprior<-2 and the mirror case, each against its no-snap control) x {oc, fwd1} x 3 universes = 24. Total 276 variants, and all of them are printed. Pass criteria, fixed in advance: same sign in the hold-out, hold-out size at least half the discovery size, hold-out |t| >= 2, at least 20 episodes in each sample, and |mean| >= 0.15%. The 14 headline rows were fixed in advance. Discovery: 2021-11-05 to 2024-12-31. Hold-out: 2025-01-01 to 2026-11-23.

results.signal: STOCKS gap z>+2 and closed below open
STOCKS gap z>+2 and closed above open
STOCKS gap z<-2 and closed below open
STOCKS gap z<-2 and closed above open
STOCKS snap-back up (gap z>+1 after prior day z<-2)
STOCKS snap-back down (gap z<-1 after prior day z>+2)

finding.strongest_effect: None held up out of sample. The largest discovery result reversed sign in the hold-out. Stocks that gapped down more than 4% and then closed above their open made +0.65% the next day in 2021-2024 (t 2.1, 66 episodes) but lost 0.88% in 2025-2026 (t -3.0, 40 episodes). That is a change of regime, not a pattern you can repeat. The most consistent same-sign cell looks like yesterday's setup. QQQ gapped up more than 1 sigma and closed below its open, and over the next 3 days it rose +1.17% vs +0.86% excess, with hit rates of 81% and 68% (unconditional about 54-58%). But its t is only about 1.7 in each sample, with 13 and 19 episodes, so it is weak. With 276 variants, about one cell like this is expected by chance.
finding.answer_to_owner: I tested 276 versions of "fade or follow the opening gap" on SPY, QQQ and 125 stocks, then checked each on 2025-2026 data it had not seen. No rule held up and also beat trading costs. Big up-gaps showed only a mild tendency to give back some gain during the day (about -0.1% to -0.5%), and not reliably. A pattern that worked in 2021-2024 flipped in 2025-2026. Yesterday is far outside the history: SPY gapping up 5% (3 sigma, right after a -2 sigma day) has happened about once in five years, so no statistic speaks to it. The crowd does react, but not the same way each time. Treat gap days as risk to manage, not a signal to trade.
caveats: Survivorship: the stocks were picked in 2026 from names popular now. Using excess over each stock's own same-sample mean reduces this but does not remove it.

The 45% split filter dropped 15 days. Several were probably real moves rather than splits (APP 2024-11-07, ARM 2024-02-08, MRNA 2026-08-19 +177%, GME 2024). Dropping them removes some of the most extreme gap events.

The hit rates in the table are pooled stock-day figures; only the means and t-statistics are clustered by date. The unconditional hit rates are averages of the discovery and hold-out values (for example 50.33/49.55 for stocks same-day), and each sample's exact figure is in results.txt. n_event_dates and n_episodes are discovery plus hold-out.
The 3- and 5-day windows overlap across nearby event dates, so their date-clustered t-statistics are somewhat too high. Episode counts are reported for this reason.

SPY and QQQ cells at 2 sigma or beyond, or 2% or more, have fewer than 10 episodes and are uninformative. Yesterday's SPY +5% gap (z 3.0) and QQQ +7.9% gap (z 3.1) have essentially no precedent in the data.
The hold-out includes the April 2025 tariff shock and the November 2026 events, and these dominate the down-gap cells. That is likely behind the sign flip in the down-gap-then-recovery next-day rows.
Prices are not adjusted for dividends, and the costs assume liquid names; options break-even hit rates of 58-65% were never reached on a usable sample.

errors_found: No look-ahead found. sigma uses closes t-20..t-1, gap and zprior are known at the open, and forward windows run from Close_t and drop spans that cross a flagged day. I reproduced their full output exactly: 276 variants, 15 dropped days, 0 rows pass.

Split filter mislabelled. All 15 dropped days look like real moves, not splits. The bars appear already split-adjusted: NVDA's 10:1 split in June 2024 shows no jump (121.0 -> 120.9 -> 121.8). So the filter removed real extreme events such as APP, ASTS x3, GME x3, MRNA +177% and UPST -56%, and caught 0 actual splits.

Their caveat says the April 2025 tariff shock and November 2026 explain the hold-out sign flip in the gap<-4% & close-above-open next-day row. I refuted this: excluding Mar 28 - Apr 30 2025 the hold-out is still -0.83% (t -2.71), and excluding November 2026 it is -0.87% (t -2.94).
Excess in the hold-out is measured against each symbol's mean over the hold-out itself. This is a mild in-sample look-ahead. It is harmless for describing effects but cannot be used for trading.
The headline hit rates are pooled stock-days, not clustered by date (they disclose this). The 3- and 5-day windows overlap, which inflates t.

QQQ z>+1 & close-below-open fwd3 (their 'most consistent' cell) is mostly market beta. Against SPY the excess shrinks to +0.49% (discovery) and +0.18% (hold-out, t 1.27), from +1.27% and +0.86% against QQQ's own mean. Shifting the signal 20 sessions later gives a larger discovery 'effect' (+1.46%, t 2.8) than the real signal, so the discovery result is regime drift, not a gap reaction.
Their reported n_event_dates and n_episodes add discovery and hold-out together, which makes the samples look larger than they are within each period.
Arithmetic check: my independent figures match theirs to within about 0.05pp (288 vs 291 discovery dates for cell A, from slightly different sigma and edge handling).
review.independent_check:
I wrote my own loop in review/indep.py and review/xsec.py, starting from the raw bars. It computes sigma from the 20 prior close-to-close returns (at least 15 valid), skips flagged days, and clusters by date. Episodes are dates at least 10 sessions apart.

Cell A, STOCKS gap<-4% & close above open, next day:
- Discovery: my +0.69%, t 2.24, 288 dates / 66 episodes vs their +0.65%, t 2.11, 291 / 66.
- Hold-out: my -0.88%, t -2.98, 207 / 40 vs their -0.88%, t -2.98, 207 / 40.
- Against SPY: +0.68% (t 2.43) in discovery, -0.74% (t -2.79) in hold-out.
- Against the same-date average of all stocks: +0.55% (t 2.24) in discovery, -0.76% (t -3.03) in hold-out.
- Hit rates: 52.0% and 42.3%, vs unconditional about 50.2% and 50.3%.
- Placebo, signal shifted 20 sessions later: -0.11% (t -0.45) in discovery and -0.29% (t -0.93) in hold-out, so nothing.
- Placebo, dates shuffled within the year: the null mean is about 0 (sd 0.11) and the real value lies outside it in both samples, but with opposite signs. The sign is unstable, so a large |t| in each half does not make this a repeatable effect.

Cell B, QQQ z>+1 & close below open, 3 days:
- Against QQQ's own mean: discovery +1.27% (t 1.79, 12 episodes), hold-out +0.86% (t 1.67, 19 episodes). Hit rates 86.7% and 65.2%, vs unconditional 53.6% and 57.3%.
- Against SPY: +0.49% and +0.18%.
- Shift-20 placebo: +1.46% (t 2.8) in discovery, -0.41% in hold-out.

Cell C, SPY same rule, 3 days:
- +0.64% (t 1.07) in discovery and +0.92% (t 1.48) in hold-out, with 12-13 episodes.
- Shift-20 placebo: +0.41% in discovery, 0.03% in hold-out.
review.corrected_statement:
No gap rule holds out of sample in a tradable way. The one large cell is stocks that gapped down more than 4% and then closed above their open. Their next-day excess was +0.69% (t 2.2, 66 episodes) in 2021-2024 and -0.88% (t -3.0, 40 episodes) in 2025-2026. This holds against the stock's own mean, against SPY and against the same-day stock average, and it is not explained by the April 2025 tariff shock or November 2026. The sign flips between periods, so it cannot be traded as one rule.

After an up-gap that closed red, SPY and QQQ drifted up +0.6% to +1.3% over the next 3 days, but on only 12-19 episodes with t below 1.8. Most of that is market beta: QQQ against SPY is only +0.18% in the hold-out. A placebo shifted 20 days reproduces it, so the evidence is weak.

Same-day fades of large up-gaps average about -0.1% to -0.5%, with |t| below 1.4, below the 0.15% cost level and not consistent across periods. For yesterday's setup (SPY +5% gap, 3 sigma, right after a -2 sigma day) there is roughly one precedent in five years, so the data says nothing about it.
review.rule_worth_paper_testing: none. At most an observation-only paper log, not a rule: on days when QQQ gaps up more than 1 sigma of its own 20-day close-to-close volatility (computed from the prior 20 sessions) and closes below its open, record QQQ's 3-day close-to-close return minus SPY's. Abandon it unless 20 or more new episodes show an excess of at least +0.15%.

teams.title: Large one-day moves: bounce, fade or drift

finding.preregistration: Written at the top of study.py before any outcome was computed, and not changed afterwards. Shock z = r_t divided by the std of the prior 20 daily returns (today excluded). Volume ratio = today's volume over the prior 20-day mean. Entry at the shock-day close, forward close-to-close returns at 1/3/5/10/20 sessions. Stock excess = stock minus SPY over the same window, then net of the unconditional excess of all stock-days in the same sample (survivorship benchmark: +0.03%/1d, +0.15%/5d, +0.68%/20d). Index excess = index return minus its own sample mean. 20 signals: DOWN z<=-2.5/-3/-4; UP z>=2.5/3/4; r<=-10%; r>=+10%; DOWN z<=-3 split by vol>=2x / <2x; UP z>=3 split the same way; SPY and QQQ <=-2%, >=+2%, <=-3%, >=+3%. Trade direction: buy down shocks, short up shocks. t-stats use date-level averages (clustered by date). Episodes = event dates at least 10 sessions apart. Discovery is 2021-11-05..2024-12-31, hold-out is 2025-01-01..2026-11-23. "Holds" = same sign in the hold-out and at least 50% of the discovery size. "Tradable" = holds, plus hold-out edge >=0.15%/trade, t>=2 and >=20 hold-out episodes. Variants tried: one specification, 20 signals x 5 horizons = 100 cells, all printed in results.txt.

results.signal: S1 DOWN z<=-2.5 (buy) [excess = per-trade edge net of unconditional]
S13 SPY r<=-2% (buy SPY) - weak, 8 hold-out episodes
S17 QQQ r<=-2% (buy QQQ) - weak, 17 hold-out episodes

finding.strongest_effect: The most consistent effect is that big up days tend to keep going, so "sell the euphoria" loses money. After a day up 3 or more of its own 20-day sigma, the stock beat SPY over the next 5 sessions by an extra 0.78% beyond the normal drift in discovery (t=2.1, 70 episodes). In the hold-out the extra was 0.52% (t=1.0, 43 episodes). The sign is the same at 1, 3 and 5 days in both samples. But it is not significant in the hold-out, and of 200 cell-tests about 9 would pass |t|>=2 by chance. So it is suggestive only, not proven. "Buy the panic" changed sign between samples: it lost in 2021-24 and gained in 2025-26, which looks like a market-regime effect rather than a stable edge.
finding.answer_to_owner: Not reliably. Over five years I looked at 125 stocks plus SPY and QQQ: what happens after panic days and euphoria days. Buying the panic lost money in 2021-24 and made money in 2025-26, so it depends on the market's mood, not on a fixed crowd reflex. Shorting the euphoria tended to lose, because big up days with news usually keep drifting up for a few days. Even that effect was too weak to count after the 2025 test period. Next-day direction was right only 43-57% of the time, below the 58-65% you need for short-dated options to pay. None of the 100 tests passed all the tradability checks. So a reaction like today's NVDA move is not predictable from these patterns alone.
caveats: The table's excess columns hold the per-trade edge: the trade direction (buy down shocks, short up shocks) times the excess over SPY, net of the universe's unconditional excess over SPY in the same sample. A negative value means the trade loses. Raw excess and the unconditional figures are in results.txt.

Survivorship: the universe was picked in 2026 from names popular now. Its unconditional excess over SPY is +0.68% per 20 days, which flatters buy-the-dip and hurts short-the-euphoria. The up-shock drift may partly be this bias.

No splits were detected. 15 genuine one-day moves beyond 45% were excluded under the pre-registered rule: APP, ARM, ASTS x3, CVNA x2, GME x3, MRNA +177% on 2026-08-19, PDD, SNAP, UPST x2. These are real news events, so the +/-10% signals miss some of the largest shocks.
Entry is at the shock-day close, which assumes you can trade at the close once you know the move. With a next-open entry the bounce figures would differ.

Multiple testing: 100 cells x 2 samples were tested. The 26 cells marked 'holds' include losing trades whose loss repeated and cells where the discovery result was about zero (for example S3 1d). None meets the tradability bar.
Index shocks are weak samples: SPY moves of 3% or more had only 2-3 hold-out episodes, and SPY at +/-2% had 7-8.
The six names with short histories are included; the 20-day sigma needs 20 prior sessions. Prices are not adjusted for dividends.
Next-day hit rates (43-57%) are below the 58-65% options break-even in every stock signal. QQQ at -2% reached 58.6% on only 29 hold-out days and was 44% in discovery.

errors_found: No look-ahead found. Sigma uses the prior 20 returns with today excluded (rolling std then shift(1)). Forward returns run from the shock-day close. The volume ratio uses the full day's volume, which is only valid for close entry, and a next-open entry check gave almost the same result (+0.70% vs +0.78% in discovery).

Benchmark mismatch inflates the headline. The event mean is an average over dates (equal weight per date), but the 'unconditional' benchmark is a pooled stock-day mean. When I shuffled the same stocks' events to random dates within the same year, the null came out at +0.31% per 5 days in discovery and +0.11% in hold-out, not 0. About 40% of the reported +0.78% discovery 'edge' comes from this weighting and from which stocks fire most, not from the shock.

Fragile to a few dates. For UP z>=3 at 5 days, the median date-level excess is only +0.12% in discovery and +0.24% in hold-out, against means of +0.78% and +0.52%. Removing the 5 best dates cuts discovery to +0.37% (t=1.17) and makes the hold-out -0.10% (t=-0.22).

The noise floor is high. The +20-session shifted placebo (no real signal) gave a hold-out 5-day excess of -0.94% with t=-2.49. A hold-out |t| of about 2.5 can therefore come from nothing, so the real hold-out t=1.0 means nothing.

Hit rates are pooled stock-days, not clustered by date, and use raw rather than excess returns. In the hold-out, pooled next-day 'up' was 46.4% but the date average was 52.7%. Because of that mismatch, the short side shows a '53% hit' while its mean loses, so the hit-rate column cannot be read as an edge.

The 'holds' test is too loose: same sign plus 50% of the size, with no significance needed. 26 of 100 cells 'hold', including cells where discovery was about 0 (S3 1d) and losing trades. Their 'strongest effect' was picked after seeing all 200 cell-tests, so it is post-hoc.

Survivorship. The universe beats SPY by +0.15% per 5 days unconditionally. Using each stock's own same-sample mean instead lowers the effect to +0.70% (t=1.92) in discovery and +0.45% (t=0.87) in hold-out.

Minor issues. pct_change on the wide frame pads across missing bars (I found 1 isolated missing bar, so the impact is negligible). The 15 dropped moves beyond 45% are removed from the signal but still sit inside other events' forward windows. No splits were found, and I agree with the 15 dropped days.
review.independent_check: My own code aligns all stocks to the SPY calendar with no fill, drops |r|>45% (15 days, same as theirs), builds z from the prior 20 returns, and clusters by date. For UP z>=3 the long-side 5-day excess over SPY, net of the universe benchmark, came out exactly like theirs. Discovery: 413 dates, 70 episodes, +0.78%, t=2.14 (theirs: edge -0.78 for the short, t=-2.14). Hold-out: 249 dates, 43 episodes, +0.52%, t=1.00 (theirs: the same). At 1 day: +0.26%/t=1.38 and +0.27%/t=1.19, which matches. DOWN z<=-3 at 5 days: discovery -0.25% (t=-0.71), hold-out +0.65% (t=1.76), which matches their sign flip. Placebos: (a) shifting the signal by +20 sessions gave 5-day discovery -0.11% (t=-0.38) and hold-out -0.94% (t=-2.49). (b) Shuffling each stock's events to random dates in the same year, 200 times, gave a null mean of +0.31% (sd 0.29) in discovery and +0.11% (sd 0.33) in hold-out. The real result beat the placebo with p=0.05 in discovery and p=0.105 in hold-out. Net of the placebo, the effect is about +0.47% in discovery and +0.41% in hold-out, neither significant once 200 tests are taken into account. The by-year means were positive in 2022-2026 (2021 has only 5 dates), but medians are small and a few dates drive the result.
review.corrected_statement: After a stock's up day of 3 or more of its own 20-day sigma, the next 5 sessions beat SPY by about +0.4-0.5% more than random days for the same stock in the same year. Discovery: +0.78% raw, against a shuffle placebo of +0.31%, p about 0.05. Hold-out: +0.52% raw, against a placebo of +0.11%, p about 0.1, t=1.0, 43 episodes. The sign is the same in both samples, but a few dates drive it: the median is only +0.1-0.2%, and dropping the 5 best hold-out dates leaves -0.10%. All this supports is that 'shorting euphoria has not paid in this survivor-biased universe'. It is not a positive, tradable momentum edge. 'Buy the panic' changed sign between samples (-0.25% in 2021-24, +0.65% in 2025-26) and is not a stable effect. Next-day direction for every stock signal stays at about 46-54%, below the 58-65% options break-even.
review.rule_worth_paper_testing: none. At most a negative filter: do not open short or bearish next-day positions only because a stock closed at z>=+3 (r_t over the std of the prior 20 returns). That filter is a risk guard, not an expected-value rule.

teams.title: Market-wide fear: breadth washouts and relief rallies

finding.preregistration: These were written at the top of study.py before any outcome was computed. Breadth uses 125 stocks (ETFs excluded). The 15 one-day moves beyond +/-45% were all set to NaN. Most are earnings or meme moves rather than true splits (SNAP, PDD, UPST x2, CVNA x2, ARM, GME x3, ASTS x3, APP, MRNA). Signals on day t, with outcomes from close(t) to close(t+h): S1 W60 = 60%+ of stocks down 2%+. S2 W40 = 40%+ down 2%+. S3 DBL40 = W40 today and on one of the prior 2 sessions. S4 BOT70 = 70%+ close in the bottom 20% of the day's range. S5 LOW30 = 30%+ at or below their prior 20-day low close. S6 = SPY 5-day return <= -4%. S7 = SPY vol5/vol60 >= 2. S8 R60 = 60%+ up 2%+. S9 RAW = 40%+ up 2%+ within 5 sessions after a W40 day (the 11-20 to 11-23 pattern). Targets are SPY, QQQ and the equal-weight universe (EW) at h = 1/3/5/10. Excess is measured over the same target's unconditional mean in the same sample. t is computed across episodes (dates 10+ sessions apart), and the primary cells are EW h=5 and SPY h=1. 'Holds' means the same sign in the hold-out at 1/3+ of the discovery size. Variants counted: 108 grid cells, plus 18 post-hoc first-date-of-episode cells, plus 2 sensitivity runs without April 2025, for 128 in total. One mid-course fix: the first run printed the pooled excess next to an episode-level t. The excess column was switched to the episode-weighted mean and the pooled figure is still printed. Thresholds were not changed.

results.signal: S3 double washout (2 W40 in 3 sessions)
S4 BOT70 (>=70% close in bottom 20% of range)

finding.strongest_effect: The most consistent effect is S5: 30%+ of stocks closing at a 20-day low. The next 5 sessions beat normal in both samples. SPY did +0.98% better than its usual 5 days in discovery (t 2.6, 17 episodes) and +1.16% in the hold-out (t 2.6, 12 episodes, hit rate 71% vs 57%). It is still fragile, for two reasons. First, the gain is much smaller when every signal day counts equally (SPY +0.17% / +0.86%) than when each episode counts once. Second, buying only on the FIRST day of each episode loses the edge: SPY +0.27% in discovery and -0.23% in the hold-out. The rebound comes from signal days deep inside long selloffs, not from the first scare. Each half of the sample has fewer than 20 episodes, so this is weak evidence.
finding.answer_to_owner: Crowd fear does repeat, but it doesn't give a clean prediction. The first day of a broad washout, like 11-20 when 72% of stocks fell 2%+, usually doesn't bounce: the following week averages slightly below normal. Only after the selling has gone on for days, with many stocks at 1-month lows, do the next 5 days tend to beat normal by about 1%. Even that comes from about 29 episodes, and it fails when you buy at the first sign. Big relief days like 11-23 (73% of stocks up 2%+) don't reliably hold. The next day is up less than half the time in 2025-26. Relief days on 11-04 and 11-09 this month faded. Nothing here clears costs reliably enough to trade.
caveats: Survivorship: the universe was picked in 2026 from names that are popular now, which flatters every buy-the-dip figure. Excess is measured against each sample's own unconditional mean, but survivorship still inflates the EW figures.

The episode counts are tiny: 3 to 24 per sample. S6 (14 episodes in total) and S7 (7) are weak whatever their t. No single half of the sample reaches 20 episodes for any washout signal except W40 in discovery.

The two samples are different market regimes. Discovery is dominated by the 2022 bear market, where washouts kept going. The hold-out is dominated by fast V-shaped recoveries (April 2025). Signals that look good only in the hold-out (BOT70 SPY 1d hit 86%, R60) rest on 5 or 6 episodes.

Episode weighting and date pooling give materially different answers. For W40 EW 5d the excess is +1.33/+0.63 episode-weighted but -0.11/-0.04 pooled. The first-date-of-episode test (post-hoc) erases most effects, and the double washout (S3) first date is negative in both samples (SPY 5d -0.87% and -2.53%).
No options-style next-day signal holds. The SPY 1d hit rates are 40-52% in discovery and do not exceed the 58-65% break-even in both samples.

The current setup (11-19/11-20 washout with SPY 5d at -8.6%, then the 11-23 relief with vol5/vol60 = 2.49) is one more observation of the same rare pattern. The forward outcomes after 11-23 are not yet in the data.
The 15 dropped moves (|1d| > 45%) are mostly genuine earnings or meme moves, not splits. Dropping them removes the stock from that day's breadth and from forward windows that span the move.
128 variants were examined in total, so a few nominal t > 2 cells are expected by chance alone.

errors_found: LOOK-AHEAD IN THE EPISODE WEIGHTING (fatal for the headline). An episode ends on the last event date that has no further event in the next 9 sessions, so the grouping uses future data. For LOW30, 'no new 20-day-low breadth for 9 sessions' means the market did not keep falling, so each episode's last date has a mechanically good forward return. SPY 5d excess on the last date of each episode is +2.92% (discovery) and +2.41% (hold-out). On all other event dates it is -0.47% and -0.11%. Single-date episodes, which are entirely 'last dates', are +2.84% and +1.09%. teams.title: Leaders and followers: does a shock in one stock predict others

finding.preregistration: I fixed these before computing any outcome, and they are written in the docstring of study.py. Groups are as given in the task. The leaders are NVDA (semis), AAPL (megacaps, the largest at the start of the sample), TSLA (EV), COIN (crypto), BABA (China) and CRM (software, the largest software name at the start). A shock is measured as z = the day's close-to-close return divided by the standard deviation of the 60 prior sessions (at least 40 required). Excess return is the stock minus SPY, then minus that stock's own mean excess within the same block (discovery or hold-out), which removes survivorship drift. Returns are signed by the shock's direction, so a positive number means the move continued. Fourteen signals: S1-S3 leader |z|>3 to followers, next-day open-to-close, next-day close-to-close and next-3-day close-to-close. S4/S5 are up-shocks only and down-shocks only. S6/S7 compare followers that under-reacted (bottom half by signed day-0 excess) with the other followers, at 1 and 3 days. S8/S9 take SPY |z|>2 days and compare the bottom-quintile laggards with the whole universe, at 1 and 3 days. S10 is SPY's own next day, as context. S11-S13 use a group-median shock (|z|>3 on the median series) and measure the members' o2c1, c2c1 and c2c3. S14 is the under-reacting-members spread after a group shock. The t-statistics use date-level averages (clustered by date). An episode is an event date at least 10 sessions after the previous one. A signal 'holds' only if the discovery |t| is at least 2, the hold-out has the same sign, and the hold-out size is at least 50% of the discovery size. It is tradable only if it holds and is at least 0.15% per trade in both blocks. Discovery runs 2021-11-05 to 2024-12-31 and the hold-out 2025-01-01 to 2026-11-23. I tried 14 variants in total and did not re-run with other thresholds.

finding.strongest_effect: None of the 14 pre-registered signals passed. The closest is S6, a within-group catch-up: on days when the leader moves beyond 3 sigma, the followers that moved least outperform the followers that moved most on the next day. The gap is +0.60% per date in discovery (t 1.56, hit rate 53%) and +0.86% in the hold-out (t 2.55, hit rate 64%). That is 107 event dates and 54 episodes. It fails the pre-registered discovery bar of t >= 2. It is also probably ordinary short-term reversal between stocks, not news spreading slowly from the leader. The plain diffusion idea, that followers keep moving the leader's way, shows nothing in discovery (-0.17%, t -0.5). In the hold-out it actually turns into reversal (-1.18% next day, t -2.05; -1.91% over 3 days, t -3.34). That pattern is only in the hold-out, so it is not reliable either.
finding.answer_to_owner: I found no reliable next-day spillover. When NVDA, TSLA, COIN, BABA, AAPL or CRM has a shock day, the rest of its group does not keep moving the same way the next day. A big SPY day does not predict that the stocks that lagged will catch up. Group-wide shocks do not continue either. From 2025 on, followers tended to reverse after a leader shock, but in 2021-2024 they did not. The one hint that showed up in both periods: after a leader shock, the group members that moved least tend to beat the ones that moved most the next day. It is not strong enough to trade. Crowds may react with the same fear every time, but the reaction is priced in the same day.
caveats: Survivorship: the universe was picked in 2026, so it is tilted toward winners. Excess returns are measured against SPY and demeaned per stock within each block to offset this. Unconditional hit rates are about 50%.

The >45% one-day filter removed 15 moves: SNAP, PDD, UPST x2, CVNA x2, ARM, GME x3, ASTS x3, APP, MRNA. Most look like genuine earnings or squeeze jumps rather than splits, and they were removed anyway as a conservative choice. No NVDA 2024 split showed up, so the data appears to be split-adjusted.

Leader choice is debatable. AAPL for megacaps and CRM for software were the largest names at the start of the sample, and MSFT or PLTR would change those events. The rule is that the leader is fixed in advance.
22 of 107 leader-shock dates were also SPY |z|>2 days, so some leader shocks are really market-wide events.
The 3-day measure adds daily excess returns together instead of compounding them. Each 3-day observation also overlaps the next ones, and t-statistics are clustered by date only.
The episode counts (34-54) are above the weak threshold of 20, but the hold-out per signal has only 20-45 event dates.
S6/S7 are long-short spreads among followers, so trading them costs two round trips, about 0.30%. They also failed the discovery bar.

Context: the data ends 2026-11-23, when NVDA went from a -5 sigma day on 11-20 to a +10.4 sigma day on 11-23 (about +31%). There are no outcomes yet for those days, and this study does not cover today's (11-24) move.

errors_found: No look-ahead in the signal itself. z uses the std of the 60 prior sessions (shift(1)), and the forward returns are correctly shifted by -1/-2/-3. Running study.py reproduces every number in their table.

S6 does not depend on the shock's sign. Signing by the leader's direction and then taking the bottom half minus the top half gives exactly 'day-0 within-group losers minus winners' whichever way the leader moved. So the 'catch-up toward the leader' story is really a cross-sectional reversal measured only on leader-shock days.

They waved S6 away as 'probably ordinary short-term reversal'. My baselines contradict that. The same losers-minus-winners spread on all days is -0.04% (discovery) and -0.01% (hold-out). On non-event days with follower dispersion at least as high as on event days it is -0.09% and +0.03%. Whatever S6 is, it is specific to the leader-shock days.

Selection: S6 was named the strongest effect after both blocks had been seen (best of 14), so its hold-out is not a clean out-of-sample test. The hold-out also shows the opposite 'reversal' pattern in S2/S3 (t -2.05/-3.34), which points to a 2025-26 regime rather than a stable law.
Small samples. My independent count is 99 event dates and 51 episodes: 32 in discovery and 19 in the hold-out. The hold-out is under 20 episodes, so it is 'weak' by the project rule.
The discovery effect is concentrated. It comes from TSLA (+2.67%, 10 dates) and COIN (+1.24%, 9 dates). AAPL (-0.29%), CRM (-0.25%), BABA (-0.06%) and NVDA (+0.09%) are flat or negative in discovery.

Execution: the c2c version needs entry at the day-0 close, which is the same price that defines the signal. The tradable next-open-to-close version is about half the size in the hold-out (+0.41%), and its medians are only +0.05% to +0.15%. Means are driven by outliers.

Minor issues. Demeaning uses each block's full-sample mean, a mild centering look-ahead that is harmless for spreads. 3-day returns are summed rather than compounded. The >45% filter dropped 15 genuine earnings or squeeze jumps rather than splits; the data appear split-adjusted, since NVDA 2024 shows no -90% day. Neither changes the conclusion.

This is a forward paper test only, kept as a watch item; no conclusion until there are at least 20 new episodes.

- **Trigger:** NVDA, AAPL, TSLA, COIN, BABA or CRM closes with |close-to-close return| / std(prior 60 daily returns) > 3.
- **Ranking:** sort that leader's pre-registered followers by day-0 return minus SPY's.
- **Trade:** at the next open, go long the equal-weighted bottom half and short the equal-weighted top half. Exit at that day's close.
- **Logging:** record the gross spread per event date and judge it net of about 0.30% cost (two legs).
- **Kill rule:** drop it if, after 20 new episodes, the mean net spread is <= 0 or t < 1.5.

teams.title: Size of moves: volatility clustering and how often crashes happen

finding.preregistration: Fixed at the top of study.py before any outcome was computed. Universe: 129 symbols (skip list removed, the 6 short-history names kept because rolling windows tolerate them). Split filter: any |close-to-close| > 45% set to missing; 15 such days dropped (APP, ARM, ASTS x3, CVNA x2, GME x3, MRNA, PDD, SNAP, UPST x2). Definitions use only data up to day t. sigma60 = standard deviation of the prior 60 sessions. 'Typical day' = mean |move| over the prior 60 sessions. A shock is |cc_t| > k*sigma60 with k = 2 or 3, either direction. Outcome = 1{|cc_t+1| > m x typical} with m = 1, 1.5, 2. Excess = outcome minus the same stock's unconditional rate in the same sample. t-statistics are on date-level averages. Episodes = event dates at least 10 sessions apart. Straddle proxy: bought at close t, settled at close t+1. Cost = 0.8 x 1.2 x EWMA(span 10) realised vol, which includes the shock day; 1.1 and 1.3 are run as sensitivity on the 3-sigma row only. P&L = |cc_t+1| - cost. Discovery 2021-11-05..2024-12-31, hold-out 2025-01-01..2026-11-23. 'Holds' means the same sign, hold-out size at least half of discovery, and at least 20 hold-out episodes. Total variants: 13 pre-registered rows, plus descriptive tables (tail frequencies, a 1-20 day persistence curve, an IV-premium sweep labelled descriptive). Nothing was added or re-tuned after seeing outcomes.

finding.strongest_effect: Volatility clustering, and it says nothing about direction. After a stock has a 3-sigma day, the chance that the next day's move is more than 1.5x its typical day rises from about 22% to 36% in the discovery sample and 45% in the hold-out. That is about +15 points in both samples, with t = 8.7 and 6.8, over 115 episodes. After a 2-sigma day the gain is +6 to +8 points. Next-day size averages 1.24x typical after a 2-sigma day (1.45x after 3-sigma). It falls to about 1.1x by day 5 and stays near 1.1x for about 20 sessions.
finding.tradable_rule: none. Clustering replicates, but it predicts size, not direction, so it gives no stock trade. A buyer of next-day straddles after a shock loses about 1.6-1.7% of the underlying per trade in both samples under the proxy (hit rate about 20%, against a 58-65% break-even). Even at an IV premium of 0.8x the forecast, the post-shock straddle still loses 0.23%. The flip side, selling straddles after a shock, depends entirely on the assumed implied-vol model, so it is not offered as a rule.
finding.answer_to_owner: Crowds are predictable in how big the moves are, not in which way. After a big shock, the next few days are much more likely to be big too, in either direction, and calm returns over roughly a week. Buying next-day options to profit from that does not work in this test, because option prices already jump after a shock and next-day moves come in at only about two-thirds of the cost. An 8% one-day SPY fall did not happen once in these 5 years. The worst day was -5.85% (2025-04-04). In longer history it is very rare: roughly 1929-33, 1987, 2008 and March 2020. Today's swing (-3.6% on Friday, +4.7% Monday) is the clustering pattern itself.
caveats: There is no option price history. The straddle cost is assumed to be 0.8 x 1.2 x EWMA10 realised vol including the shock day, so the straddle result shows only how far real moves fall short of what that model implies. Real implied vol after shocks may rise less, and then a buyer could do better than shown. Bid-ask spreads on options, which would hurt a buyer further, are ignored.
Pooled tail frequencies are per stock-day and dominated by volatile names. Survivorship: the universe was picked in 2026 from popular, often high-volatility names.

SPY-only rows have 39 episodes and do not replicate (discovery excess +0.6 points, hold-out +15.5, t 1.9), so read them as weak. The index-level clustering evidence comes from pooled stocks, not from SPY alone.

15 split-like days were dropped by the 45% rule. Some were probably real moves, such as the GME and ASTS spikes, and splits smaller than 45% (for example 3-for-2) would get through the filter. Prices are not adjusted for dividends.
Shocks are two-sided and measured against a trailing 60-day sigma. The 1x typical baseline is 39% rather than 50% because the distribution is skewed (mean |r| is above the median).
'Holds' on the straddle rows means the loss replicates, not that a profitable effect exists.

General knowledge, not computed from this data: S&P 500 closes of -8% or worse since 1950 are about six days (1987-10-19 at -20.5%; 2008-09-29, 2008-10-15 and 2008-12-01 at about -9%; 2020-03-12 at -9.5%; 2020-03-16 at -12%). They were more frequent in 1929-1933.

errors_found: Straddle result depends on the assumed cost. The cost is 0.8 x 1.2 x EWMA10 vol including the shock day. With span 10 the shock carries about 18% of the variance weight, so after a 3-sigma day the assumed cost (mean 5.50%) is far above the realised next-day move (3.12%). If the cost uses pre-shock vol (EWMA through t-1, or sigma60) with the same 1.2x premium, the post-3-sigma straddle turns POSITIVE: +0.30%/+0.38% (disc/hold, t 2.1/2.8), and +0.78%/+0.80% at a 1.0x premium. The finding 'buying post-shock straddles loses 1.6-1.7%' is an assumption, not a result. Neither sign can be decided without real option quotes. Post-earnings IV crush (most shocks are idiosyncratic, probably earnings) means the shock-inclusive model probably overstates the buyer's cost.

The all-days straddle baseline loses -0.53% at 1.2x by construction (cost 0.96 x RMS vol, against E|r| of roughly 0.8 x sigma). At 1.0x the loss is only -0.08%/-0.06%. Labelling straddle rows as 'holds out of sample' is meaningless: the model replicates itself.

As general knowledge, not from this data: one-day 8%+ index falls happened only in 1929-33, October 1987, October-November 2008 and March 2020.
review.rule_worth_paper_testing: No stock trade rule. The only thing worth a paper test is measurement, not trading. On each session when a liquid optionable name closes more than 3x its trailing 60-day sigma (either direction, not an index), log the real quoted ATM straddle mid near the close on the nearest expiry. Compare it to the realised |close t+1 - close t| and to the 1-day share of the straddle's value decay. Collect at least 20 distinct episodes before drawing any conclusion. Only then decide whether the realised move exceeds the quoted straddle mid net of the spread. Until real quotes exist, no straddle buy or sell rule is supported.

finding.preregistration: The rules were written at the top of study.py before I computed any outcome, and I did not change them afterwards. There are 18 rules for each of 3 assets (SPY, QQQ, and EW, the equal-weight average of 125 stocks), so 54 tests and no other variants. The rules: day of week Mon to Fri (R01-R05); the 3-session cumulative return ending the Wednesday before US Thanksgiving (R06, 2021-2025, n=5); the Black Friday half day (R07, n=5); each of the last 3 sessions of the month (R08) and the first 3 (R09); each session of the Mon-Fri week containing the third Friday, using the prior session when that Friday is a holiday (R10); the session after monthly expiry (R11); the next day after 3, 4 or 5 or more consecutive down closes (R12-R14); the next day after 3 or more up closes (R15); the session after a Friday above +2% (R16) or below -2% (R17); and Turnaround Tuesday, a Tuesday whose prior session was a down Monday (R18). The outcome is the close-to-close return minus the same asset's unconditional mean in the same period (times 3 for R06). The t-statistic is computed on one value per date, so it is clustered by date. Discovery is 2021-11-05 to 2024-12-31 and the hold-out is 2025-01-01 to 2026-11-23. I applied Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR 10%) and Holm (5%) across the 54 discovery p-values. A rule "holds" only if its discovery q is below 0.10, the hold-out has the same sign, and the hold-out mean is at least 50% of the discovery mean. Episodes are events at least 10 sessions apart.

finding.strongest_effect: The strongest effect is SPY bouncing on the day after 4 or more consecutive down closes. In discovery it beat SPY's unconditional mean by 0.62% (t=3.6, 33 dates, 18 episodes, up 66.7% of the time against 52.6% on all days, BH q=0.055). In the hold-out it beat the mean by 0.88% (16 dates, but only 10 episodes, t=1.1, up 68.8% against 53.5%). It is the only one of the 54 tests that passes the pre-registered bar, and it is still weak. Fewer than 20 episodes in each sample, and the hold-out t is only 1.1. QQQ shows the same pattern only in milder form. Its 3-down version gives +0.39% in discovery and +0.37% in the hold-out, but its 4-down version fades to +0.09% in the hold-out. For the equal-weight stock universe the rule does nothing (-0.02% / -0.11%). Holm finds 0 of 54 significant. Disc and hold-out agree in sign in 33 of 54 tests, where coin-flipping would give 27.
finding.tradable_rule: Paper-test only, and it is weak. At the SPY close, if SPY has closed lower than the prior close on 4 or more consecutive sessions, buy SPY at that close and sell at the next session's close. Repeat every day the streak continues, and stop the day after the first up close. The historical edge is +0.6% to +0.9% per trade before costs, which is well above the 0.15% cost. The hit rate is about 67-69%, above the 58-65% options break-even, but on only 28 episodes overall (10 in the hold-out). Keep paper-logging until there are at least 20 more episodes before trusting it.
finding.answer_to_owner: Mostly no. I tested 18 popular timing rules on SPY, QQQ and an equal-weight basket, 54 tests in all. Day of week, turn of month, opex week, Turnaround Tuesday and the Friday-move rules flip sign between 2021-24 and 2025-26. They are noise. The one pattern that survives is a modest bounce in SPY after 4 or more straight down days, about +0.6-0.9% the next day, up roughly 2 times in 3. Crowds overselling and then partly reversing fits that. But it rests on only 28 episodes, it does not work for single stocks, and it failed for QQQ at the 4-day level. Last week SPY fell 4 days running and then rose 4.7% on Nov 23, which matches the pattern. The Thanksgiving-week rally rests on just 5 holidays.
caveats: Multiple testing: 54 tests. Only 1 passes BH at 10%, with q=0.055, so it is borderline. Holm at 5% finds 0.

The one surviving effect has 18 discovery and 10 hold-out episodes, both under 20, so it is weak by the project rule. The hold-out t is only 1.12. The streak events overlap, since a 6-day streak fires on 3 consecutive days.

Thanksgiving has only 5 events (4 discovery, 1 hold-out), so it cannot be tested. SPY rose in the 3 pre-holiday sessions in all 5 years, from +0.1% to +3.1%. Black Friday was mixed. Interesting, but not evidence.
Hold-out Monday strength (+0.23% SPY, t=2.1) and Thursday weakness (-0.23%) did not appear in discovery. They look like regime noise from 2025-26.

Survivorship: the EW universe was picked in 2026, so its unconditional mean is flattered. That is why results are measured as excess over each asset's own mean. Down-streak bounces in the index probably also reflect 2022-2026 being a rising market that recovered from every dip. A long bear market could break the rule.

15 one-day moves beyond +/-45% were dropped from the stocks as possible splits: SNAP, PDD, UPST x2, CVNA x2, ARM, GME x3, ASTS x3, APP, MRNA. Several of these are probably genuine earnings or meme moves rather than splits. The split check affects only the EW series.
The data ends 2026-11-23, so today's (11-24) fall is not in the sample. Prices are unadjusted for dividends. All returns are close-to-close, and an open-to-close or intraday entry would differ.
The 125 stocks in EW include the six short-history names, which enter the average only on dates when they have data.

errors_found: No look-ahead found. The streak signal uses closes up to day t and the outcome is day t+1 (shift is correct). The Friday and Turnaround Tuesday rules are aligned correctly. The calendar dates do not depend on outcomes. SPY and QQQ are one value per date, so their t-statistics really are date-level. There were 0 split-like moves (>45%) in SPY or QQQ.

The hold-out result for the 'strongest effect' depends on one outlier. Of the 16 hold-out trades, 2025-04-09 (the tariff-pause day, +10.45%) is the largest. Without April 2025 the hold-out mean falls from +0.88% to +0.24% (t=0.49). Without the top 2 outcomes (+10.45% and the +4.66% excess on 2026-11-23) it is -0.08%. Because the 'holds' verdict is driven by the mean, it rests on a single news day.

The discovery edge is concentrated in the 2022 bear market. The top 3 outcomes are all from 2022 (Mar 8, Aug 9, Oct 12). The hit rate of 22/33 against a 52.6% base gives a one-sided binomial p of only 0.073. The hold-out hit rate of 11/16 against 53.5% gives p=0.165.

Overlapping signals: a 7-day streak fires 4 times. Counting only the first day each streak reaches 4 gives disc n=22, +0.50%, t=2.49 and hold n=11, +1.10%, t=1.14. The hold-out is still dominated by April 2025.

The narrative about last week is wrong. SPY fell 7 sessions in a row (Nov 12 to Nov 20), not 4. The rule as written bought at the Nov 17, 18, 19 and 20 closes. Those trades returned -0.31%, -1.96%, -3.64% and +4.71%, a net loss of about 1.3% over 4 trades before the bounce paid. So the recent episode is not clean support for the rule.

Multiple testing and nesting. k=3/4/5 are nested variants of one idea, and the winner sits at BH q~0.055 (p=0.001 x 54). Holm finds 0 of 54. The shift-20 placebo still shows +0.30% in discovery, so part of the discovery 'edge' is a general high-volatility 2022 rebound drift, not anything specific to the streak.
Minor: the excess is measured against the period mean including the event days (negligible). The R06/R07 Thanksgiving rules (n=5) should not have been counted as testable in the BH family.

review.corrected_statement: Over 2021-2026, SPY's next-day return after 4 or more consecutive down closes has averaged above normal: +0.62% in 2021-24 (t=3.6, but only 18 episodes and mostly from 2022) and +0.88% in 2025-26 (t=1.1, 10 episodes). The 2025-26 figure depends almost entirely on the 2025-04-09 tariff-pause day. Without April 2025 it is +0.24% (t=0.5), and without its 2 best days it is -0.08%. The median hold-out excess (+0.52%) and the hit rate (11/16) still point the same way but are not significant (binomial p=0.17). The best the evidence supports is a weak, non-significant tendency for SPY to bounce after sharp multi-day selloffs in high-volatility regimes. It is not a reliable streak-specific edge, and none of the 54 calendar rules survives Holm. The Thanksgiving and other calendar rules are noise or untestable (n=5).
review.rule_worth_paper_testing: Paper-log only, and with no prior that it works. At each SPY close where SPY has closed lower than the previous close on 4 or more consecutive sessions, record a hypothetical long SPY from that close to the next close. Log only the first day each streak reaches 4, so there is one trade per streak. Pre-commit to evaluating after 20 new streak episodes. Count it as alive only if the mean after the 0.15% cost is > 0, the median is > 0, and the result survives dropping its single largest trade. Do not use short-dated options on it: the hit rate on independent episodes has a 95% CI that easily includes the 58-65% break-even.

synthesis:
**Short version:** six research teams tested five years of data on SPY, QQQ and 125 stocks, and an independent reviewer re-ran every study. The data does not show which way the market moves next. Crowd fear is real, but it gets priced in on the same day. The one thing you can predict is that a big day is likely to be followed by more big days, in either direction.

**1. What is predictable**
- **Big days come in clusters (strong).** After a stock moves 3 times its usual daily size, the next day's move is more than 1.5 times normal 36% of the time in 2021-24 and 45% in 2025-26. On an ordinary day that figure is 22%. This rests on 115 independent episodes (t 8.7 and 6.8) and held in both periods. The next day is about 1.45x a normal day on average, falls to about 1.1x by day 5, and stays near 1.1x for about four weeks. It tells you how big, not which way. Buying next-day straddles (paying for a big move in either direction) to profit from it lost about 1.6-1.7% per trade in both periods, because option prices already jump after a shock. So it does not clear costs. Use it to size positions, not as a signal.
- Nothing about direction passed review.

**2. What is not**
- **"Buy the panic."** It lost money in 2021-24 (-0.25% over 5 days) and made money in 2025-26 (+0.65%). That depends on the market's mood at the time, not on a fixed crowd reflex.
- **"Sell the euphoria."** Shorting stocks after big up days tended to lose, because they kept drifting up by about 0.4-0.5% over 5 days. But a handful of days drive that result, so the honest reading is only "don't short just because a stock spiked".
- **Market-wide washouts.** The headline "+1% bounce after a mass selloff" came from a grouping error that used future information (dates were grouped knowing the selling had already stopped). With that fixed, nothing is left.
- **Leader spillover.** An NVDA shock does not carry over into the rest of its group the next day.
- **"It should have stayed green today."** History doesn't support that expectation:
  - Gap-ups usually gave back 0.1-0.5% during the same day, though not reliably.
  - In 2025-26, relief days soon after a washout were followed by an up day for SPY only 43% of the time (2021-24: 52%).
  - Monday's setup has essentially no precedent. SPY opened 5% higher (3 times its normal daily move) right after a -2 sigma day, which has happened about once in five years.
  - A pattern that made +0.65% in 2021-24 lost -0.88% in 2025-26. The crowd reacts, but not the same way each time.

**3. How often the big days happen**
- **SPY:** not one day of -8% in these five years. The worst was -5.85% on 2025-04-04. Since 1950 the S&P 500 has fallen 8% or more in a day about six times: 1987, three days in 2008, and twice in March 2020. Before 1950, mostly 1929-33.
- **Single volatile names:** an 8% day is far more common. Across the pooled stocks, about 1 day in 8 is more than twice that stock's typical move. After a shock that rises to 1 in 4 to 1 in 3.
- So "8% is doable" holds for a single high-volatility stock, especially right after a shock. For the index it is a once-in-a-decade event.

**4. Rules worth a paper test (watch-only; none is proven)**
- **A. Catch-up after a leader shock (weak; only 19 episodes in 2025-26).**
  - Trigger: NVDA, AAPL, TSLA, COIN, BABA or CRM closes more than 3 sigma from its usual move.
  - Entry: at the next open, buy the half of that leader's group that moved least against SPY, and short the half that moved most.
  - Exit: that day's close.
  - Kill it if, after 20 new episodes, the average spread after about 0.30% costs is 0 or below, or t is under 1.5.
- **B. QQQ up-gap that closes red (log only; weak, 12-19 episodes).**
  - Trigger: QQQ opens more than 1 sigma higher and closes below its open.
  - Record: QQQ's next 3-day return minus SPY's.
  - Kill it unless 20 or more new episodes show at least +0.15%.
- **C. Risk filter, not a trade.** Never open a short or bearish next-day position only because a stock closed 3 sigma or more higher. Also shrink position size for about 5 days after any 3-sigma day, because of the clustering in section 1.

**5. Why the market fell this morning**
News coverage puts it down to chip and AI selling. NVDA was down about 5% after Monday's +31%, Micron about -8% and AMD about -9%. Monday's Nvidia-driven relief rally, which had already closed below its open, faded, and rate and inflation worries ahead of the December Fed meeting added pressure. Profit-taking fits the pattern, but no source says so directly, and a reported Iran sanctions story is unconfirmed. Confidence: medium-low.
